segments.caption: Why does the bell curve show up everywhere?
Even when the data isn't shaped like a bell?
The answer is the Central Limit Theorem.
Here's what it says, in simple words.
Take many random samples, and find the average of each one.
Those averages will form a bell curve, even if the original data isn't a bell.
You just need big enough samples, usually 30 or more.
Let's see it with an example.
Here are the salaries in a city.
Most people earn a little, and a few earn a lot.
So the data is skewed, not a bell.
Step 1: pick 30 people at random, and find their average salary.
Step 2: pick another 30, and find their average.
Step 3: repeat this again and again, and plot every average.
Look! The averages form a bell curve.
Why does this happen?
In a random group of 30, the few huge salaries get mixed with many ordinary ones.
So the extremes cancel out, and most averages land near the middle.
Two bonus facts.
The bell is centred on the true average of the whole city.
And bigger samples make it narrower, so your estimate gets more precise.
So remember the Central Limit Theorem.
Many samples, one average each, and those averages make a bell curve, whatever the original shape.
That's why a survey of a few thousand people can describe a whole country.
Quick quiz!
Some data is very skewed. You take many samples of 50, and plot their averages.
What shape will you see?
A bell curve!
With big enough samples, the averages form a bell, whatever the original shape.
In future videos, we'll explore other kinds of distributions.
Follow for data science made simple!
